{{nihongo|'''Takeda Katsuyori'''|武田 勝頼||extra=1546 &ndash; 3 April 1582}} was a Japanese ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' (military lord) of the {{ill|Sengoku period|ar|فترة سينغوكو|arz|فتره سينجوكو|be|Перыяд Сэнгоку|bg|Сенгоку|bn|সেনগোকু যুগ|bo|སེན་གོའི་དུས་མཚམས་|ca|Període Sengoku|ckb|سەردەمی سێنگۆکو|cs|Období Sengoku|de|Sengoku-Zeit|eo|Epoko Sengoku|es|Período Sengoku|et|Sengoku ajastu|eu|Sengoku aroa|fa|دوره سنگوکو|fi|Sengoku-kausi|fr|Époque Sengoku|ga|Tréimhse Sengoku|glk|سنگؤکۊ زمات|he|תקופת סנגוקו|hu|Hadakozó fejedelemségek kora (Japán)|id|Zaman Sengoku|is|Sengoku-öldin|it|Periodo Sengoku|ja|戦国時代 (日本)|ka|სენგოკუს პერიოდი|kk|Сэнгоку дәуірі|ko|센고쿠 시대|lt|Sengoku laikotarpis|ms|Zaman Sengoku|nl|Sengokuperiode|no|Sengoku-perioden|pl|Sengoku (okres)|pt|Período Sengoku|ro|Perioada Sengoku|ru|Период Сэнгоку|sh|Sengoku razdoblje|simple|Sengoku period|sk|Obdobie Sengoku|sq|Periudha Sengoku|sr|Сенгоку период|sv|Sengoku|th|ยุคเซ็งโงกุ|tl|Panahong Sengoku|tr|Sengoku Dönemi|uk|Період Сенґоку|ur|سینگوکو دور|uz|Sengoku davri|vi|Thời kỳ Chiến Quốc (Nhật Bản)|wuu|战国时代（日本）|zh|战国时代 (日本)|zh_min_nan|Sengoku sî-tāi|zh_yue|戰國時代 (日本)|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period}}, who was famed as the head of the [[Takeda clan]] and the successor to the legendary warlord {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}}. He was son-in-law of [[:en:Hojo Ujiyasu|Hojo Ujiyasu]], ''daimyō'' of Hojo clan.

==Early life==
He was the son of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Shingen}} by the daughter of {{ill|Suwa Yorishige (daimyo)|en|Suwa Yorishige (daimyo)|qid=Q2511179|lt=Suwa Yorishige}} ({{ill|Posthumous name|ast|Nome póstumu|ca|Nom a títol pòstum|cs|Posmrtné jméno|de|Postumer Titel|es|Nombre póstumo|fa|نام پسامرگ|fr|Nom posthume|hi|मरणोपरांत नाम|hr|Imina|id|Nama anumerta|it|Nome postumo|ja|諡|ko|시호|lt|Pomirtinis vardas|ms|Nama pusaka|nl|Naamgeving van Chinese keizers|no|Posthumt navn|pl|Imię pośmiertne|pt|Nome póstumo|ru|Посмертный титул|sh|Posthumno ime|simple|Posthumous name|sl|Posmrtno ime|sv|Postumt namn|th|สมัญญานาม|tr|Ölüm sonrası adı|uk|Посмертне ім'я|ur|پس مرگ نام|vi|Thụy hiệu|wuu|谥号|zh|谥号|zh_classical|諡|zh_min_nan|Sē-hō|zh_yue|謚號|qid=Q696100|lt=Posthumous name}}:{{nihongo|''[[Suwa-goryōnin]]''|諏訪御料人||extra=real name, Koihime}}).<ref name="Sato">{{Cite book |last=Sato |first=Hiroaki |title=Legends of the Samurai |publisher=Overlook Duckworth |year=1995 |ISBN=978-1-59020-730-7 |page=209 |author-link=Hiroaki Sato (translator)}}</ref> Katsuyori's children included Takeda Nobukatsu and Katsuchika.<ref name="harimaya.com">{{Cite web|url=http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/html/takeda.html|title=兵庫県西部、播磨地方の情報を中心に日本の旅の想い出を発信しています|language=Japanese|website=www2.harimaya.com}}</ref>

Katsuyori, first known as {{nihongo|'''Suwa Shirō Katsuyori'''|諏訪四郎勝頼}}, succeeded to his mother's [[Suwa clan]] and gained Takatō Castle as the seat of his domain.

After his elder brother {{ill|Takeda Yoshinobu|en|Takeda Yoshinobu|qid=Q837273|lt=Takeda Yoshinobu}} died, Katsuyori's son Nobukatsu became heir to the Takeda clan, making Katsuyori the ''de facto'' ruler of the Takeda clan.<ref name="battles">{{cite book |last1=Turnbull |first1=Stephen |title=Battles of the Samurai |date=1987 |publisher=Arms and Armour Press |isbn=978-0-85368-826-6 |location=London |pages=79–94}}</ref> Takeda Katsuyori built {{ill|Shinpu Castle|en|Shinpu Castle|qid=Q11502234|lt=Shinpu Castle}}, a new and larger castle at Nirasaki and transferred his residence there in 1581.

==Military life==
In 1569, Katsuyori defeated [[Hojo Ujinobu]] at {{ill|Siege of Kanbara|en|Siege of Kanbara|qid=Q2659520|lt=Siege of Kanbara}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jalan.net/kankou/spt_22382af2170020709/ |title=蒲原城|publisher=じゃらん|language=ja|access-date=25 July 2019}}</ref>

In 1572, Katsuyori successfully took a [[Tokugawa clan]] possession in the {{ill|Siege of Futamata|en|Siege of Futamata|qid=Q1014528|lt=Siege of Futamata}}, and participated in the {{ill|Battle of Mikatagahara|en|Battle of Mikatagahara|qid=Q690464|lt=Battle of Mikatagahara}} against the Oda-Tokugawa alliance.<ref name="Turnbull2">{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |publisher=Cassell & Co. |year=1998 |ISBN=1-85409-523-4 |page=219,222–223,230}}</ref>

In 1573, Katsuyori took charge of the Takeda family after the death of Shingen and fought the [[Tokugawa clan]].

In 1574, he {{ill|Siege of Takatenjin (1574)|en|Siege of Takatenjin (1574)|qid=Q4540826|lt=captured Takatenjin castle}}, which even his father had not managed to do. This gained him the support of other members of the Takeda clan.

In 1575, he suffered a terrible loss at the {{ill|Battle of Nagashino|en|Battle of Nagashino|qid=Q428369|lt=Battle of Nagashino}}, defeated by one of the earliest recorded uses of [[:en:Volley fire (infantry tactic)|volley fire]] (by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|qid=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga}}'s 3,000 muskets), and losing a large part of his forces as well as a number of Takeda's generals and retainer.<ref name="Steve">{{cite book |last1=Turnbull |first1=Stephen |title=The Samurai |date=1977 |publisher=Macmillan Publishing Co., Inc. |isbn=978-0-02-620540-5 |location=New York |pages=156–160}}</ref>

In 1578, Katsuyori incurred the wrath of the {{ill|Later Hōjō clan|en|Later Hōjō clan|qid=Q431928|lt=Hōjō family}} by helping {{ill|Uesugi Kagekatsu|en|Uesugi Kagekatsu|qid=Q1376605|lt=Uesugi Kagekatsu}} against {{ill|Uesugi Kagetora|en|Uesugi Kagetora|qid=Q1190934|lt=Uesugi Kagetora}} who was {{ill|Hōjō Ujiyasu|en|Hōjō Ujiyasu|qid=Q943643|lt=Hōjō Ujiyasu}}'s seventh son, adopted by and heir to {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|en|Uesugi Kenshin|qid=Q311080|lt=Uesugi Kenshin}}, that initiated the {{ill|Battle of Omosu|en|Battle of Omosu|qid=Q610329|lt=Battle of Omosu}} in 1580 against [[:en:Hojo Ujimasa|Hojo Ujimasa]].

In 1581, Katsuyori {{ill|Siege of Takatenjin (1581)|en|Siege of Takatenjin (1581)|qid=Q2275430|lt=lost Takatenjin fortress}} by {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|qid=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}, the siege ended with the deaths of 680 men of {{ill|Okabe Motonobu|en|Okabe Motonobu|qid=Q1073455|lt=Okabe Motonobu}} garrison.<ref name="Cassell">{{cite book |last1=Turnbull |first1=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |date=2000 |publisher=Cassell & C0 |isbn=1-85409-523-4 |location=London |page=231}}</ref>

In 1582, Katsuyori {{ill|Siege of Takatō (1582)|en|Siege of Takatō (1582)|qid=Q2901847|lt=lost Takatō castle}} by {{ill|Oda Nobutada|en|Oda Nobutada|qid=Q2446917|lt=Oda Nobutada}}, the only Takeda stronghold in {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=Shinano province}} to put up any resistance to Nobunaga's final invasion of Takeda domain, the castle was taken on March the 2nd 1582.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Ōta |first=Gyūichi |title=The chronicle of Lord Nobunaga |date=2011 |publisher=Brill |others=J. S. A. Elisonas, Jeroen Pieter Lamers |isbn=978-90-04-20456-0 |location=Leiden |pages=426–441 |oclc=743693801}}</ref>

==Death==
{{Main|Battle of Tenmokuzan}}
After Katsuyori {{ill|Siege of Takatenjin (1581)|en|Siege of Takatenjin (1581)|qid=Q2275430|lt=lost Takatenjin fortress}} and {{ill|Siege of Takatō (1582)|en|Siege of Takatō (1582)|qid=Q2901847|lt=Takatō castle}}, many clans like Kiso and Anayama withdrew their support for Takeda. The Oda-Tokugawa alliance advanced into {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|qid=Q858076|lt=Kai Province}}, and laid siege to {{ill|Shinpu Castle|en|Shinpu Castle|qid=Q11502234|lt=Shinpu Castle}}, Katsuyori was unable to hold the castle with his remaining 300-400 men, so he set fire to Shinpu Castle and fled into the Tenmoku mountain. Later, his forces were destroyed by the combined armies of {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|qid=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga}} and {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|qid=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} at the {{ill|Battle of Tenmokuzan|en|Battle of Tenmokuzan|qid=Q1113509|lt=Battle of Tenmokuzan}}, after which Katsuyori, his wife, and his son committed ritual suicide, known as {{ill|Seppuku|en|Seppuku|qid=Q133462|lt=Seppuku}}.<ref name=battles/><ref name=Turnbull2/>{{rp|231}} It was the end of [[Takeda clan]].

The nun {{ill|Rikei|en|Rikei|qid=Q3432034|lt=Rikei}} wrote an account of his wife's suicide and, pitying them, wrote several verses in their honour.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sato |first1=Hiroaki |title=Japanese Women Poets |date=2008 |publisher=M.E. Sharpe, Inc. |isbn=978-0-7656-1784-2 |location=Armonk |pages=137–139}}</ref> of Takeda Katsuyori at Tenmokuzan|alt=|center|426x426px]]

== Spouse ==
[[File:Hojo Masako (Takeda Katsuyori's wife).jpg|thumb|Keirin'in (Katsuyori's wife) carrying a {{ill|Naginata|en|Naginata|qid=Q546116|lt=Naginata}} in the {{ill|Battle of Tenmokuzan|en|Battle of Tenmokuzan|qid=Q1113509|lt=Battle of Tenmokuzan}}.]]

=== Toyama Fujin ===
Takeda Katsuyori married Toyoma Fujin, the adopted daughter of {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|en|Oda Nobunaga|qid=Q171411|lt=Oda Nobunaga}}. She died while giving birth to their son Nobukatsu in 1567.

=== Keirin'in ===
Katsuyori later married Keirin'in, daughter of {{ill|Hōjō Ujiyasu|en|Hōjō Ujiyasu|qid=Q943643|lt=Hojo Ujiyasu}}. They had a son and two daughters. In 1582, when Keirin'in was 19, Katsuyori was decisively defeated by Oda Nobunaga, and they had to flee. However, Katsuyori was resigned to die and urged her to leave him. She refused and killed herself (''[[:en:Jigai|Jigai]]''), along with Katsuyori in the {{ill|Battle of Tenmokuzan|en|Battle of Tenmokuzan|qid=Q1113509|lt=Battle of Tenmokuzan}}. Both of his sons died in the battle.
